intro: Look up at two tiers of arches striding across the valley between two hills. This is the Valens Aqueduct, in İstanbul province, dating from AD 373. It was the last link in a 250-kilometre line from the Thracian springs, and it was kept in repair and in use through the Ottoman centuries.
history: The aqueduct was completed in AD 373 under the emperor Valens. It formed the last link inside the city of a long line that ran all the way from the springs of Thrace, carrying water over the valley between two hills to the cisterns. In Ottoman centuries it was repaired again and again, and so the city's water system kept working for hundreds of years.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the Two tiers of arches and the Roman water line they carry. Look for the Traces of Ottoman repairs, and then walk through the Passage beneath the arches.
facts: Did you know? The surviving stretch is about 900 metres long, and today one of the city's busiest roads runs beneath its arches. Yet the aqueduct was only the last link of a water line hundreds of kilometres long, reaching back to the springs of Thrace. It was maintained under the Ottomans too, so the city's water ran along this Roman line for centuries.
outro: This brings our tour of the Valens Aqueduct to an end. Please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These arches have carried a city's water for centuries; let them stand for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
